recordings.text: Whoa, fork time! One piece is threatening a whole bunch of targets in the very same move, and that's so much fun to see.
Whoa, a fork just opened up for the other side: a single piece of theirs could bounce at a bunch of targets in one go. Little lesson: count which squares hit two things at once.
Ooh, look! Hiding in a different move was a fork, one piece bouncing at a whole bunch of targets. That fork zips by this time.
Wow, a piece is stuck to its king! It can't budge from where it stands, because moving would leave its king wide open.
Ooh, check this out! The other side's next move could freeze a piece in place, pinned in front of its own king.
Hey, peek at this! Another move had a pin waiting, and that piece would have been frozen right in front of its king. This move goes a different way.
Whoa, look, a skewer! The front piece is under attack, and when it scoots away, the piece behind it gets hit on the same line.
Whoa, two pieces are lined up like ducks, ready for the other side to skewer. If the front one hops away, the back one could get hit.
Whoa, a hidden line! A different move set up a skewer: shoo the big piece in front out of the way, and its buddy in back would have been the one to fall.
Wow, watch this! First the defender gets captured, and now the piece it was protecting has nobody looking after it.
Ooh, a defender is up for capture now. Lose it, and whatever it was protecting is left without a guard.
Ooh, tricky stuff! With another move, a defender would have been knocked out, its job left undone. This move skips that trick.
Whoa, back-rank alert! The king is walled in by its own team, and this move zeroes in right there.
Ooh, look: that king is stuck behind a wall of its own guys. Now the other side could sneak in a back-rank mate.
Ooh, check this out! Another move had a back-rank mate ready, against a king hemmed in by its own team. This move went a different way.
Whoa, look at that pawn run! Zooming up the board, and once it lands on the last rank, it turns into a whole new piece.
Whoa, zoom zoom: a pawn on their side has a clear run at the last rank. Promotion could be coming for the other side.
Look over here! A stronger move would have rolled out the red carpet for a pawn heading to promotion. This move keeps that little pawn parked.
Whoa, tricky! One piece hops out of the way, and boom, the hidden piece springs into action. That's what a discovered attack looks like!
Whoa, a piece of theirs is parked in front of another. If it hops aside, the one behind gets to attack. Keep an eye out for that hidden pounce!
Hey, look closer! A different move had a discovered attack, one piece hopping aside so the one behind could pounce. That trick never gets sprung here.
Woo, double trouble! One move, and out come two threats, and both of them want an answer.
Whoa, the other side has a double attack available now: one reply, and a pair of threats pops up. Answering both is the hard part.
Ooh, look! A stronger move had a double attack, a pair of threats landing together. That chance zips by in this game.
Ooh, watch the defender! It gets tugged off its job, and the spot it was covering is wide open now. Deflection, spotted!
Whoa, that defender is working hard, and the other side can tug it off its job. A deflection like that leaves its spot uncovered.
Hmm, a crafty idea! Another move could have yanked a defender off duty and left its post empty. That deflection waits for another day.
Ooh, wide open! Nobody was looking after that piece, so it gets gobbled up, free and clear.
Hey, look closer! Another move could have gobbled up a piece with no guard at all. That snack zips by here. Easy habit: look for anything unguarded before every move.
Whoa, nobody's guarding that piece anymore, and nothing stops the other side from gobbling it up.

Ah, found the problem! That piece only had one real defender, and this move sends it away, so the other side can capture. Quick tip: whenever a defender wanders off, count up everything it used to protect.

Ah, look closely! Something got threatened by the opponent's last move, and that threat is still sitting there after this one, so a piece can be captured. Little lesson: start by asking what their last move threatens.
Hmm, that first capture sure looks yummy, but then the other side recaptures, and what it grabs back is worth more. Easy habit: tally the whole swap, every grab from both sides.
Hi there, minor piece! It leaves its starting spot and joins in.
Another move would have gotten a sleepy minor piece off the back row and into the action.
Zoom zoom! The rook gets a file with no pawns at all, not one of either color.
With a different move, a rook could have zoomed onto a file with no pawns anywhere on it.
Zoom, look where the rook landed: a semi-open file! Its own pawns are nowhere on it, while one or more enemy pawns are still hanging around.
Ooh, a semi-open file was there for a rook with another move, empty of its own pawns while an enemy pawn still sits on it.
Whoa, look at that pawn go free! Not one enemy pawn stands in its path, on its file or on either file next door.
A different move would have freed up a passed pawn, with nothing from the enemy pawns standing in its way, there or on the files next door.
Hop, hop! That passed pawn is inching toward the far end of the board.
With another move, the passed pawn would have marched closer to promotion.
Hmm, this pawn has no pawn friends on the files beside it. That makes it an isolated pawn.
With a different move, a pawn would have ended up isolated, all alone without pawn buddies on the neighboring files.
Look at that, the piece finally has a defender! It's not out there by itself anymore.
Another move would have sent a defender over to an unguarded piece.
Hmm, this piece is standing out there unguarded now. Good to notice, even though unguarded doesn't mean it can be won.
Another move would have left a piece with nothing guarding it, and that alone doesn't mean it could be won.
The king gets a brand-new spot it's legally allowed to step on. More wiggle room!
With a different move, the king would have had one more legal spot to scoot to.
The king castles, and in hops the rook to keep it company. King and rook, both on the move together, wheee!
Another choice was castling, so king and rook both move in a single turn.
This capture breaks up a bishop pair, and now one side's bishops can only walk on one color.
Another move would have swiped a bishop, and the other side's bishop buddies would be split apart.
Stack attack: two same-colored pawns now sit on a single file. That's a doubled pair!
With another move, two same-colored pawns would have stacked up on one file.
Whoa, this is a biggie: a forced mate is now waiting for the other side. Let's follow the attack move by move and find where the defense ran out.
Whoa, check this out! A forced checkmate was ready and waiting, and this move wanders off elsewhere. That finish is worth finding on the board.
Wow, what an offer! The other side is allowed to take the material, but in the line we checked, the idea survives the capture.
Whoa, a lifeline! Out of the moves we checked, all the rest were losing; this one move alone keeps things playable.
Whoa, how about that! Among all the moves we checked, the others were losing, and just this one kept the edge alive.
Hmm, let's peek at their reply. Something can be snapped up by the other side right now.
The other side's best answer comes with check! First things first: the king needs taking care of.
The engine's heart is set on another move here. Let's set it up on the board, side by side with this one, and watch the replies!
Hmm, a little leak: the engine's best would have kept a bit more value. The reply explains what slipped.
Whoa, strong move alert! The engine barely finds anything better.
Ooh, solid! The engine has a slight favorite elsewhere, yet nearly all the value is still there.
Ooh, a famous opening has this very move in it. We've got a map for now!
So long, opening book! From here on, it's brand-new territory.
Hey, you bounced back, teammate! That earlier setback is in the rearview now, and this move gets the game playable again. That's real fighting spirit!
That earlier setback didn't stop you: playable again! The other side's errors gave you a hand, and you were ready to grab it.
Yippee! The opponent's last move left a chance, and you snapped it up right away.
Oopsie, a missed chance! A goodie was sitting there after the opponent's last move, and this move sniffs right past it. Let's rewind a move and spot it.
Hey, we've met this one before! A slip like this already happened earlier in this game. Let's study those moments as a group.
Hooray, a defender is back on duty for that piece that was all alone earlier!
No single big mistake here, just a pile of little concessions adding up, and this is another one. Let's walk back through that whole stretch together.
That edge stuck with you all the way to the win! Great teamwork from start to finish.
Hey, this same trouble is hiding in your other saved games too! Let's study them together and practice it.
Checkmate! The king is trapped, and you won it!
Checkmate. The king got cornered with zero legal moves. That one stings; let's rewind together and hunt for where the defense could hold.
Draw game! Nobody wins this time, but there's still good stuff to learn from the earlier moves.
Ready, set, look! Check out the position, and pick a move whenever you like.
Not that one, and that's okay! Have another peek and try something else.
Hmm, that attempt didn't bring anything back. Let's try that move one more time!
Woo! Forced checkmate turns up in the saved engine analysis, and the side that just moved is the one delivering it!
Eek, the saved engine analysis has bad news for whoever just moved: a mating attack is coming from the other side, and it can't be stopped.
Count the pieces when the saved line is over: the side that made this move comes out with more material than at the start.
Count the pieces when the saved line is over: the side that made this move comes out with less material than at the start.
Accepted, yay! Thumbs up from the exercise. Nothing in the moves shown spells out a clear tactical reason, so we won't invent one.
Not this one for the exercise, sorry! And the moves shown keep their tactical reason a mystery.
Ding! That move is on the saved answer list. For this exercise, nothing else gets the checkmark.
That move isn't on the saved answer list. It might be perfectly fine chess; this exercise is looking for a different answer.
Give the move a good look, and then let's bounce along to the next position.
Good one! Keep the why tucked away for next time.
Saved and done! Your review dates are exactly the same.
Woo, solved! Relearning is still on the list for this one, though.
Okay, here's our starting spot, before any of these moves happen.
Onward! Let's peek at the board now.
Check, check! Before anything else, the king needs looking after.
Out of check the king goes, safe and sound. Hop, hop!
All the way up the board goes the pawn, and on the last rank it turns into a brand-new piece. Woo!
Last rank reached, new piece made, and check given too!
Ta-da, a brand-new piece on the last rank, and it's checkmate! Game over for that king.
Busy little pawn! Last rank reached, shiny new piece made, and its king escapes check at the very same time.
Gobble! Off the board goes a piece.
Gobble, with check on top!
Gobble, checkmate! The king is out of places to go.
Gobble and escape: something gets captured, and the king gets out of check!
Chomp, then promote! A capture on the last rank, and up pops a brand-new piece.
One little pawn does a triple trick: it grabs a piece, becomes a new one, and gives check, wow!
Chomp on the last rank, promote, and that's mate! The king is out of places to go.
The pawn captures on the last rank and promotes, and its own king is rescued from check at the same moment.
Castling, and surprise: that rook says check! How fun!
Castling, then boom: checkmate! The other king is completely stuck.
A single piece aims at several targets together, and then it gobbles one up. In this example, the fork wins material overall!
Nope, no capture for that piece. Its king sits behind it on that line, so it's stuck in a pin.
Scooting away isn't allowed for that attacked piece: its own king is lined up behind it. Its king has to stay shielded no matter what.
Capturing back is off the table for the defenders, since each one is pinned to its king. In the line shown, that side comes out with extra material.
The pinned piece has to stay on that line, or its king would be left open. A few moves later, it's captured anyway.
The front piece scoots off the line, and its buddy in back gets captured on that very line.
The king is checked and has to step out of the way, and then the same attacker grabs whatever was hiding behind.
Poof, the only guard disappears first. Then, later on in these moves, what it was guarding gets captured too.
Off goes the defender, lured away, and then whatever it was protecting gets captured.
A blocker hops out of the way, which clears a lane for a different piece to make a capture.
Hop! One piece scoots aside, and surprise, the piece behind it says check. Boom!
Whoa, check times two! Two pieces are attacking the king together, so the king itself has to move.
Double trouble: the moving piece makes one attack, a hidden piece makes the other, and that second one wins its target.
The pawn promotes, and in this example the material count tips that side's way.
That piece had no guard, so it gets captured, and the side that took it comes out ahead in material in this example.
Thanks to the opponent's previous move, the attacking piece is out of a relative pin. Nobody came to the target's rescue, so the line shown ends with it captured.
The other side gets to try the marked reply, no rule against it. Let's play it on the board and find out what it does!
Before moving, scan for any of your pieces that could be taken with no good recapture waiting.
Before a quiet move, sniff around for any enemy piece left with no guard.
Hunt for forcing moves that let a single piece threaten two juicy targets.
Before a pinned piece moves, take a peek at what's lined up back there: the king, or a bigger prize than the pinned piece.
Watch for attacks that zip through the first target and hit something more valuable hiding behind it.
Before you trade off a defender, make a little list of its current guard duties.
When a blocking piece moves, sniff along every lane it leaves wide open.
Hunt for one move that packs two threats inside. Checks and lines that just opened up count as threats too!
Before a back-rank defender moves, double-check that the king has somewhere to run.
Pawn race tip: count the steps it needs to promote, then look hard at every pawn push that forces things.
Before a defender moves, list everything it's guarding, because that's what it would leave behind.
Add up the whole swap: everything that gets grabbed, then whatever the recapture takes back.
See if a forcing trade could lure a defender away from some other job it's doing.
Saved answers are the only ones this exercise accepts. Lots of other legal moves can be lovely chess, too!
Every reply in this line is a strong one. Some of those replies had other options, though.
Material changes are counted only along the line shown, starting at its first move. How much each piece is worth is in the written explanation.
